title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 9: The PCGG Cases: Recovery of Ill-Gotten Wealth
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's summary of five unanimous decisions he wrote in his five years on the Court involving the PCGG and its crusade to recover the alleged ill-gotten wealth of former President Marcos, his family, nominees, cronies and associates.

The sequestration line of cases, which turned on strict compliance with the PCGG's own Rules: a writ signed by a mere representative and task force head was void (Dio Island Resort), a writ signed by one commissioner before the Rules took effect was valid because rules are not retroactive (Provident International Resources), and identical writs signed by one commissioner after the Rules took effect were void (Imelda Cojuangco).

The jurisdictional and procedural holdings: that the Sandiganbayan's authority over ill-gotten wealth is exclusive, plenary and all-embracing and extends to all related incidents, that a third party claiming ownership of sequestered shares must be allowed to intervene (First Philippine Holdings), and that a judicial action impleading a party only by an amendment filed three years later fails the six-month requirement of Section 26, Article XVIII of the Constitution.

Chavez v. PCGG, which upheld a citizen's standing and the Court's venue, affirmed the State's duty to disclose ongoing negotiations on matters of public concern, and voided the 75-25 General and Supplemental Agreements with the Marcos heirs for seven legal flaws ranging from unauthorized criminal immunity and tax exemption to the waiver of future claims and the absence of presidential approval.
sub_topics: He introduced the group as five unanimous PCGG cases from his five years on the Court, naming Chavez v. PCGG -- which invalidated the Marcos heirs' Compromise Agreements -- as perhaps the most significant.

In First Philippine Holdings the PCGG sought reconveyance of 6,299,177 sequestered PCIBank shares allegedly acquired by the Romualdez spouses through Equities and Narciso as dummy buyers with negligible cash out, and the Sandiganbayan had already let Equities intervene as claimed owner.

The Court held First Philippines must also be allowed to intervene under Rule 12, since intervention settles the whole controversy in one action and the company was so situated as to be adversely affected by any disposition of shares in the custody of the court.

It held the Sandiganbayan had jurisdiction, following PCGG v. Pena and six cases decided with it, because exclusive jurisdiction extends not only to the recovery of ill-gotten wealth but to all incidents arising from or related to such cases, which cannot be litigated in another forum.

In Dio Island Resort a Sequestration Order of April 14, 1986 had been issued by Atty. Jose Tan Ramirez, a PCGG representative and head of its Region VIII task force, against a corporation never impleaded in the later Complaint.

The Court held the assets were not properly sequestered, because Section 3 of the PCGG Rules left no room for interpretation and under no circumstances could a freeze or sequestration order be issued by one who was not a commissioner; the PCGG's later confirming Resolution did not cure it, and Ramirez lacked even specific authority at the time.

It confirmed that Section 2 of Executive Order No. 14 lodged all PCGG cases and all related incidents in the Sandiganbayan's exclusive and original jurisdiction, subject only to review on certiorari by the Supreme Court, and that any act transgressing the PCGG's objectives is subject to remedial action there.

In Provident International Resources the Writ of March 19, 1986 against the corporations' assets had been signed by one commissioner only, but the Court upheld it because it preceded the PCGG Rules of April 11, 1986, and no statute, decree, ordinance, rule or regulation is given retroactive effect unless explicitly decreed.

It also found compliance with Section 26, Article XVIII, since under Republic v. Lobregat corporations formed from ill-gotten wealth need not be impleaded merely on that ground, and the corporations were listed in the original Complaint and later impleaded by amendment.

In Imelda Cojuangco the Orders of May 9, 1986 against Prime Holdings and its PTIC shares, signed solely by Commissioner Mary Concepcion Bautista, were void because the Rules then in force required two commissioners' signatures, which are the best evidence by which the target can visually verify approval and validity.

There the Court also found no proper judicial action: the 1987 Complaint impleaded none of the private respondents, PTIC's listing covered only shares illegally acquired by the original defendants, and the April 23, 1990 amended Complaint impleading PHI and the Cojuangcos could not relate back beyond the constitutional six-month period.

In Chavez v. PCGG, the Marcos heirs and PCGG Chairman Magtanggol Gunigundo had executed two December 1993 Agreements settling all claims and splitting $356 million in Swiss deposits 75-25 in the government's favor, then submitted them to the Sandiganbayan for approval.

Francisco I. Chavez sued as taxpayer, citizen and former official to compel disclosure and prohibit a private compromise; the Court upheld his standing as a citizen asserting a public right, and noted the intervention of the heirs of Edgar Jopson, salvaged during martial law, made the question moot.

It held itself the proper venue, because the Petition reached beyond the Agreements already drawn to any future settlement and to the precise scope of the constitutional provisions on public transactions.

On disclosure it held the State must publicly disclose matters of public concern, that documents in public officers' hands in connection with official functions must be accessible, and that the framers meant to include negotiating terms, so the PCGG had to disclose sufficient information on any proposed settlement.

It grounded this in President Aquino's February 1986 mandate to recover ill-gotten properties, her first executive orders having the nature of legislative enactments, making such matters imbued with public interest.

It then voided the Agreements for serious legal flaws: criminal immunity under EO 14 could not cover the principal defendants, who had given no vital information; and the promised tax exemption usurped a power vested in Congress, would have been class legislation failing equal protection and uniformity, and fell outside the internal revenue commissioner's powers to compromise or abate.

It further held that binding the government to cause the dismissal of pending cases encroached on judicial power, since dismissal lies within the court's discretion once jurisdiction attaches; that the waiver of all claims 'whether past, present, or future, matured or inchoate' was contrary to the Civil Code's bar on waiving future fraud and licensed fraud without liability.

It condemned the waiver as a palpable violation of due process and equal protection and a dangerous precedent inviting officials to amass funds illegally and compromise their liability for a portion of the loot.

Finally it faulted the Agreements for fixing no definite period for the parties' prestations, for stating no standards beyond the unexplained 75-25 ratio for the Swiss deposits, warning that manifestly disadvantageous arrangements invite indictment under the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, and for lacking President Ramos's stipulated approval -- though even with it the Agreements would still have been invalid.

stances.claim: A sequestration writ is valid only if issued in strict compliance with the PCGG Rules in force at the time, so a representative could not issue one and, after April 11, 1986, one commissioner's signature could not suffice.
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-application across paired cases, distinguishing them by date rather than by result, with non-retroactivity supplying the dividing line

stances.claim: The State must disclose matters of public concern, including the negotiating terms of any proposed settlement of ill-gotten wealth, subject only to reasonable safeguards for the national interest.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional interpretation grounded in framers' intent and in the policy of transparency as a check on those entrusted with public affairs

notable_anecdotes: He framed the chapter by noting that during his five years in the Court he had written a number of unanimous PCGG decisions, singling out Chavez v. PCGG as perhaps the most significant for invalidating the Marcos heirs' Compromise Agreements.

He recorded that the PCGG, alerted when the validity of its Region VIII representative's writ was challenged at hearing, passed a Resolution confirming, ratifying and adopting as its own all writs signed by Ramirez and Abella to remove any doubt -- an effort the Court found unavailing.

He noted that the heirs of Edgar Jopson, who was salvaged during the martial law years, intervened in Chavez to join in praying for disclosure, rendering the question of the petitioner's standing moot.
He observed that the Agreements set no period for performance, remarking that it could have taken a lifetime for the Marcoses to submit an inventory of their total assets.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' collected five unanimous decisions CJP wrote on the Presidential Commission on Good Government and its crusade to recover the alleged ill-gotten wealth of former President Marcos, his family, nominees and cronies. In First Philippine Holdings he held that a company claiming ownership of 6,299,177 sequestered PCIBank shares had to be allowed to intervene before the Sandiganbayan, since intervention settles the whole controversy in one action and the shares were in the custody of the court, and that the Sandiganbayan's jurisdiction over ill-gotten wealth is exclusive, plenary and all-embracing, reaching every related incident. Three sequestration cases turned on the PCGG's own Rules: the writ against Dio Island Resort was void because it was issued by a regional representative rather than a commissioner, and no later ratifying resolution could cure it; the writ against Provident International Resources, though signed by only one commissioner, survived because it predated the Rules of April 11, 1986 and no rule is given retroactive effect unless explicitly decreed; and the writs against Prime Holdings and its PTIC shares, signed after the Rules took effect by a single commissioner, were void because two signatures are the best evidence of the Commission's approval, while the amended complaint impleading the Cojuangcos three years later could not satisfy the six-month requirement of Section 26, Article XVIII. The chapter closed with Chavez v. PCGG, where the Court upheld a citizen's standing and its own venue, held that the State must disclose matters of public concern including the negotiating terms of any settlement, and voided the December 1993 General and Supplemental Agreements splitting $356 million in Swiss deposits: the PCGG could not grant criminal immunity to principal defendants, could not grant tax exemptions vested in Congress, could not promise the dismissal of pending cases, and could not waive future claims -- a waiver the Court called a dangerous precedent effectively ensconcing the Marcoses beyond the reach of the law.
